ut_upper_jungle.blurb: A high-elevation cliff band on the Aquarius Plateau in south-central Utah, reached by forest road from the Pine Lake side at roughly 10,400 feet. The 25 climbs are mostly traditional lines on long cracks and faces, plus a few bolted routes, with grades running from easy fifth class up through the low 5.11s and the bulk sitting around 5.10. The rock is a rough, broken volcanic tuff; quality varies and loose sections are common, so a helmet and small-to-medium wires are wise. The cliffs hold morning shade but warm up by late morning, and the thin-air altitude keeps it a summer and early-fall destination.
ut_upper_jungle.parking_note: Drive the forest road toward Pine Lake to the hairpin turn where the Lower Jungle lot sits; the Upper Jungle signed trailhead is about 100 meters farther up the road.
ut_upper_jungle.approach: A short, cairned trail drops from the road down to the base of the cliff.

ut_bioturbation_wall.blurb: A long sandstone wall in the Indian Creek canyon system of southeast Utah, sitting just to the right of Way Rambo. All 25 climbs are crack and trad lines, spread widely along the cliff rather than bunched together. Grades are mostly 5.10 to 5.12, with the largest group at 5.11 and one easier line near 5.9, so it suits climbers comfortable on moderate Creek splitters who want some room to themselves. Expect the usual Wingate-style desert cracks, with sandy sections and lichen-streaked patches on a few lines. Bring a full rack of cams and plenty of tape.

ut_south_facing_wall.blurb: The first wall hikers meet on the trail up to the Hinterlands, a limestone sport area on the bench above Provo and just north of Rock Canyon. Twenty-four bolted lines face south, so the wall soaks up sun and is most pleasant from late fall through early spring. A handful of short, easy lines sit on the far left, while the main body is steady 5.10 and 5.11 climbing with a few 5.12s on the right. The hike up is steep and switchbacked, so it is a workout before the first pitch, but the crowds stay light and the valley views are good.

ut_ed_and_terry_wall.blurb: A west-facing wall in Rock Canyon above Provo, perched directly over the Red Slab. It holds 24 climbs, mostly traditional with some sport and top-rope options, and the grade range is wide: a few scrambles and low-fifth-class lines, a solid middle of 5.6 to 5.8, and a handful of 5.10s and 5.11s. Reaching it means passing the top of the slab and scrambling a fixed-rope fourth-class step, which adds a few minutes and thins the crowd. Loose rock can drop onto people below, so helmets are a good idea. It makes a quieter alternative when the slab below is busy.

ut_melting_mud_wall_the.blurb: The eastern-most wall of the East Hellgate cluster in Little Cottonwood Canyon near Alta, at about 8,500 feet. It is sport-only, with 24 bolted lines of limestone that demand edges and pockets. Grades start around 5.8 and reach the low 5.12s, but most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.11, so strong intermediates will feel at home. Lines are long, well bolted and often sandy in spots, and the wall draws more traffic than its neighbors. A helmet is a sensible choice here, and the walk from the road is short and steep.

ut_hideout_wall.blurb: A remote Wingate sandstone wall on the northern edge of the La Sal Mountains in southeast Utah, at roughly 6,500 feet. Nearly all of the 24 routes are traditional crack climbs, with one aid line; the grades cluster at 5.10, with a few 5.9s and 5.11s and a single route in the low 5.12 range. The approach is long and rugged, with no formal trail, and a small forest campground sits below the cliff. It rewards climbers who want solitude and a bit of adventure rather than a quick sport day, and the sandstone should never be climbed while wet.
